newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Senate rejects relaxed abortion law.
newsitem.headline: Polish Senate rejects relaxed abortion law.

text.p: Poland's Senate rejected a liberalised abortion bill on Thursday.

The bill now returns to the leftist-dominated 460-seat lower house which had passed it at the end of August by 208 votes to 61 and could force it through by approving again with a two-to-one majority.
The 100-seat Senate rejected the bill by 50 to 40 with two abstentions in a vote that split the ruling coalition.

The larger coalition party, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance, backed the liberalisation. Most of the Polish Peasant Party's senators voted with Church-linked opposition parties against the measure.

The present law, passed under a strongly Catholic government soon after the fall of communism, allows abortion only if pregnancy threatens a woman's life or health, results from rape or incest, or when the foetus is irreparably damaged.
The amendments would let women end pregnancies before the 12th week if they were too poor to raise a child or if they had other personal problems.
Parliament passed similar amendments in 1994 but they were vetoed by then President Lech Walesa, a devout Catholic.
Aleksander Kwasniewski, who beat Walesa in last year's elections, says he is ready to sign the new law.

Before the Senate vote the Peasant Party, keen to keep its options open for next year's general elections, established contacts with the rightist Solidarity movement and said cooperation was possible on several issues, including abortion.
